chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the `row["requested_by"] != canon.agent` owner gate and drops `agent` from `Canon.record`, but it adds no wave/coordinator or successor-lane relationship to the bound record. The bug calls for spendability by “any successor lane of the same wave/coordinator,” not by any differently named agent. Input: lane A in wave W1 receives an APPROVED ask id for a gate-skip on item I; unrelated lane B in wave W2 re-runs the same verb/item/target/args/state (the gate outcome and findings are identical, and the new `test_an_approval_binds_the_action_not_the_agent` exercises exactly this with `thief`) and supplies A’s ask id. The new digest matches because it no longer contains agent (or the legacy fallback matches using `requested_by`), so B spends A’s approval. The prior refutation that “there is no wave/coordinator field in the approval canon” states the gap rather than answering it: those fields must be added to the bound record if the same action can be re-run outside the successor wave.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:70

chunk_findings.detail: The current record still emits `"v": 1` while omitting `agent` (the prior untriaged finding shows the version was reverted from v2 back to v1 without restoring the agent or adding a v1-with-agent fallback). A pre-fix unspent approval row stores a digest over `{"v":1, "agent": <requesting agent>, ...}`; after this change, a successor re-running the exact same command gets `{"v":1, ...}` without `agent`, so the stored digest does not match and the previously granted approval remains unspendable. The new migration test does not answer this: it creates its “legacy” digest with the newly added `canon.digest_named` helper rather than using a digest produced by the old pre-fix serializer, so it exercises the new helper, not the old stored byte format.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/canon.py:Canon.record

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises that “a WIDENED action (a different item/gate/args/verb) is refused”, but the test body only asserts that `C.spend(thief, _canon(agent="thief"), filed.id, now=T0 + 1)` succeeds and records the consumer. It no longer attempts any different item/gate/args/verb or asserts a refusal; the old negative assertion was removed. A change that drops all digest-scope checks except `agent` would still pass this test, so the migration away from agent binding is not actually protected against accidentally widening approvals beyond the stated fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_consume.py:test_an_approval_binds_the_action_not_the_agent

chunk_findings.detail: The flipped `assert not err` validates that `mallory` can spend an approval requested by `bot` (`ask(proj, "bot")`), but nothing establishes `mallory` as a successor lane or a member of the same wave/coordinator. The test therefore blesses arbitrary cross-agent spending by any agent that supplies the existing `ask_id`, not the intended “successor lane of the same wave/coordinator” scope. The earlier refutation (“there is no wave/coordinator field”) describes the gap rather than answering it: the fix removes the agent binding without adding the missing relationship check, and this regression test codifies that over-broad behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the owner-gating check (`row["requested_by"] != canon.agent`), allowing any agent to spend any pending approval as long as the digest matches. However, there is no verification that the spending agent is actually a "successor lane" or authorized within the same wave/coordinator. An arbitrary attacker or unrelated agent (such as `"thief"` or `"mallory"`) can intercept and consume any unspent approval issued in the system, provided they can match or guess the command arguments, item, and state, completely bypassing the intended operational isolation between independent workflows.

data.context: B86be969daf: a claim.force/complete.force approval was owner-gated to its requester and expired unused when that lane died. Options were (a) any-agent spend on the exact approved action, (b) successor lane of the same wave/coordinator only, (c) longer unspent TTL. The operator chose (a).
data.decision: An unspent ddflow approval may be spent by ANY agent (not only the filing agent) when it re-runs the exact approved action (same verb/item/target/args/state digest). The owner-gate is relaxed: the digest binds the action, not the actor.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_pre_fix_agent_bound_approval_is_still_spent_by_a_successor` does not actually reproduce a pre-fix approval: it builds the “legacy” digest by calling `canon.digest_named("asker")`, a method this same change introduces in `canon.py`. On the unfixed code that digest method does not exist, so the regression test dies with `AttributeError` before exercising the owner gate. More importantly, if `digest_named` were implemented incorrectly — for example, returning the new agent-less `canon.digest` — this test would still pass, because both the stored approval and the spend path would use the same broken helper, while real pre-fix rows whose stored digest includes the requesting agent would remain stranded. The migration regression test should hardcode the pre-fix legacy digest/record instead of invoking the new helper.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_consume.py:161

chunk_findings.detail: The intent and description state that unspent approvals expire in 3600s (`use_ttl_s=3600`), and that an expired approval prevents stranding or should be rejected. However, `ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py` removes the owner-gating check and accepts any successor agent without implementing or checking any time-to-live (`use_ttl_s=3600` or expiration relative to `now` or `timestamp`), leaving unspent approvals valid indefinitely rather than expiring after 3600 seconds as specified. Given an approval requested at `T0`, calling `C.spend` or `C.operator_gate` at `T0 + 4000` succeeds despite exceeding the 3600s TTL.

chunk_findings.detail: The test and its docstring claim that a widened action (different verb/item/gate/args/state) is refused even by a same-named process, but the body only calls `C.spend` with `_canon(agent="thief")`, which has the same action as the filed approval, and asserts it succeeds. It never submits a different `verb`, `item`, `target`, `args`, or `state` and asserts `not got.ok`. A future implementation that removes action matching while still ignoring the agent would pass this test, so the test does not actually pin the action-binding property it is named for.

chunk_findings.detail: These new expectations reuse the old adversarial agents `thief` and `mallory` but make no setup call establishing either as a successor lane in the requesting bot’s wave/coordinator. The old tests explicitly used these same agents as non-owners who must fail. An implementation that keeps the intended restriction to actual same-wave/coordinator successor lanes would make both assertions fail, while an implementation that simply drops the owner gate and lets any agent spend passes. The regression suite therefore encodes the over-broad “any agent” behavior instead of the “successor” behavior and would not catch that security regression.
